findings.claim: All 42 practice questions across lessons 1-7 are labelled “20 marks — Extract Analysis” and carry the ladder “Top band (17–20) … Band 4–1: Progressively less detailed.”
findings.truth: The 19th-century prose question is a single source-based response worth 40 marks (a printed extract plus the whole novel). Label rewritten to “40 marks — Extract and whole-text response” and the ladder rescaled to five equal house bands: Top 33–40, Upper-mid 25–32, Mid 17–24, Lower-mid 9–16, Low 1–8.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md lines 427–444 (19th Century Prose, 40 marks, 20% of the qualification, source-based response, AO1/AO2/AO3)

findings.claim: “I can be rid of Mr Hyde… whenever I choose” — repeated in lessons 2, 5 and 7 in content, in a knowledge-check stem and in three flashcards.
findings.truth: Jekyll says “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr. Hyde.” The reordering is a misquotation, and the knowledge check was testing the invented wording.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.3 line 649: “I will tell you one thing: the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr. Hyde.”

findings.claim: Flashcard: “Which Enfield exclamation calls Hyde primitive?” → “God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic.”
findings.truth: Utterson says it, walking away after meeting Hyde in ch.2. Enfield never speaks the line. The lesson body attributes it correctly, so only the flashcard is wrong.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.2 lines 504–506: “‘There is something more, if I could find a name for it. God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic, shall we say?’ said the perplexed gentleman” (Utterson).

findings.claim: “Poole tells Utterson: ‘That’s not Jekyll’s voice — it’s Hyde’s!’” — in the lesson body, in a knowledge-check stem and in a flashcard.
findings.truth: Utterson cries the line at the locked door after the voice inside begs for mercy. Poole’s own words are “was that my master’s voice?” and “master’s made away with”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.8 line 1561: “‘Ah, that’s not Jekyll’s voice—it’s Hyde’s!’ cried Utterson. ‘Down with the door, Poole!’”

findings.claim: Quoted twice as “Hyde’s powers had grown with the sickliness of Jekyll”, plus a flashcard and a mark-scheme note.
findings.truth: The sentence is “The powers of Hyde seemed to have grown with the sickliness of Jekyll.”

findings.claim: Flashcard: “Which shared description shows Jekyll and his servants recognising horror?” → “They were both pale; and there was an answering horror in their eyes.”
findings.truth: The sentence describes Utterson and Enfield in the street after Jekyll slams the window. No servant is present.

findings.claim: Enfield “witnessed a man ‘calmly trampl[e] over a child’s body’”.
findings.truth: Stevenson’s word order is “trampled calmly over the child’s body”. Students who memorise the lesson version write the quotation wrongly.

findings.claim: “Bones audibly shattering” given as a quotation in the body, a key fact, a mark scheme and a flashcard.
findings.truth: The text reads “under which the bones were audibly shattered”. The lesson quotes the passage correctly once and then re-quotes it wrongly four times.

findings.claim: Under the heading “Chapter 5: After the Murder”: Jekyll’s two months of peace, “the animal within me licking the chops of memory”, and the involuntary park-bench transformation. A knowledge check matches “Chapter 5” to “Jekyll appears to reform”.
findings.truth: Jekyll’s reform and the two quiet months open ch.6 (‘Remarkable Incident of Dr Lanyon’); ch.5 is the incident of the letter. Both quoted lines and the park-bench change come from Jekyll’s statement in ch.10.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg headings at lines 839 (ch.5), 1027 (ch.6); ch.6 line 1047 ‘for more than two months, the doctor was at peace’; ch.10 lines 2407–2410

findings.claim: Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859) “suggested that humans were descended from apes”.
findings.truth: Origin does not trace human ancestry; Darwin left that to The Descent of Man (1871), and the claim is that humans and apes share an ancestor, not that one descends from the other.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Origin_of_Species (human evolution deliberately left out; ‘light will be thrown on the origin of man’)

findings.claim: Glossary tooltip: allegory = “A story that investigates the inner workings of a character’s mind and moral conflicts.”
findings.truth: That defines a psychological study. An allegory is a story whose characters and events stand for deeper ideas.
findings.evidence: term definition; the lesson’s own glossary entry is closer

findings.claim: Flashcards in lessons 1 and 7 answer “Which adjective… / Which single word…” with the bare word “Troglodytic”.
findings.truth: House rule: a one-word answer is only allowed when the question opens What is / Who was / When / Name. Answers expanded to name the speaker and the sense.

findings.claim: “His rational, legal mind makes him [Utterson] a reliable narrator.”
findings.truth: Utterson narrates nothing. Chapters 1–8 are third person focused through him; the only first-person narrators are Lanyon (ch.9) and Jekyll (ch.10). Lesson 6 states this correctly, so the unit contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg chapter headings; L6 content_html ‘The first eight chapters are third-person narration focused through Utterson.’

findings.claim: “the fog still slept on the wing of the morning”.
findings.truth: “The fog still slept on the wing above the drowned city.”

findings.claim: Flashcard: “Which Utterson line shows Victorian refusal to probe uncomfortable truths?” → “The more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask.”
findings.truth: Enfield says it in ch.1; Utterson replies “A very good rule, too”. The lesson body and the knowledge check attribute it correctly, so only the flashcard is wrong.

findings.claim: “You will be assessed against … AO1 … AO2 … AO3 (context), and AO4 (written accuracy)”, and a knowledge check asking for the fourth objective with “AO4” marked correct.
findings.truth: The 19th-century prose section assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3 only. Written accuracy is assessed on the post-1914 section and on Shakespeare, not here, so nothing on this question rewards spelling and grammar. The knowledge check marked a false answer correct.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md line 442 ‘Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3’; lines 423 and 360 place AO4 on the post-1914 and Shakespeare sections

findings.claim: Description reads “exam strategy for Eduqas Component 2 Section B”; the exam tip says “the 40-mark Eduqas question”.
findings.truth: House rule bans naming the board in lesson prose and bans component codes. Replaced with “the 19th-century prose question” and “this 40-mark question”. The 40-mark total was already right.
findings.evidence: unit house rules; CHECK_PROMPT banned-string list

findings.truth: The section is 40 of the paper’s 120 marks in 150 minutes, so the fair share is about 50 minutes. The advice under-timed the answer.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md lines 392–452 (2 hours 30 minutes; three 40-mark sections)

findings.claim: Lesson 3 is titled ‘Chapters 5-8: The Unravelling’ but its first section covers ch.6 and ch.10 material, and ch.5 (the letter, Guest and the handwriting) is never taught in the unit.
findings.truth: The title stays defensible once F9 lands. Recording it because ch.5 content is a genuine gap, not an error — a later build could add the handwriting scene.

summary: Seven lessons checked against the Gutenberg text and the spec. Six misquotations and three misattributed lines found (the troglodytic exclamation, the Queer Street rule and the ‘not Jekyll’s voice’ cry all given to the wrong speaker), plus two knowledge checks that tested invented wording and one that marked AO4 correct on a section where it is not assessed. Every practice question in the unit was labelled 20 marks with a malformed ladder; all 42 rescaled to the real 40-mark question. No lesson was error-free, but lesson 4 carried only the practice-label fault.
